verdict.rationale: The README outlines the control path. The ESP32 board acts as the mouse and runs a hid_bridge with BLE configuration, plugs into the phone over USB-C or a Lightning camera adapter, and drives the iOS pointer through AssistiveTouch, which the app calibrates. It does not explain the input path in depth, so it only partly covers how inputs reach the device. missing for 10: a detailed description of the HID report and protocol, an explicit explanation of how the app→BLE→board→USB HID→AssistiveTouch chain works end to end, how taps and swipes are translated into pointer events, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As a developer, the control path (USB HID, accessibility APIs, OS input events) is documented, so I know how inputs reach the device

citations.quote: The board is now the AirPlay receiver and the mouse, and the agent runs in an iPhone app on the same phone.
Let Me Use the Pointer — turn on AssistiveTouch; the app calibrates the pointer by itself.
USB-C models plug in directly; Lightning models need a Lightning to USB Camera Adapter. The phone powers the board.
Always build with flash.sh: it applies the BLE buffer sizes in hardware/hid_bridge/nimble_cfg.h.
Debugging without the phone app: hardware/tools/board_test.py plays the app over BLE from a Mac
